A romance writer. would not fail to make it one. or other of them, but Idonot like romances, except it be those of Richardson. Iam writing history ; whether this history be interesting or uninteresting, is the least of my care. My plan was to adhere to truth, and I have executed it. —~No.—He is dead or alive then as you please. I might stop this phaeton, and make the. friar and his companion give rise to a series of events which would disappoint you of hearing both James's amours and those of his Master; but I despise such resources, I see that it only requires a little imagination and some command of language to frame a romance. Let us adhere to truth and till James recovers from his sore throat, let us permit his Master to speak. The Chevalier added: in fifteen days! the term is very short. You are either in love or you ate not; in fifteen days! what do you propose to do?—I replied, without any hesitation, to the Chevalier, that I would . withdraw.— Withdraw! you are not in love then ?—I am in love; but I have relations, a name, an estate, and some pretensions; and I never can resolve to bury all these advantages i in the arms of 2 cit’s pert little daughter. —And shall Het them know this ?—If you please. But, Chevalier, the sudden and scrupulous delicacy of these people surprises me. They have allowed their daughter to accept my entertainments, and they have left me séte-a-1éte with her twenty times. I will not believe, I will not deny all that is said of her; but you will agree that these parents ought to have bethought themselves sooner of becoming jealous of the honour of their daughter.
